Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

```pddl
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---

    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t

    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
```

not acknowledged within 1 clock tick of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

table in the payments database. The payout ledger entry and the id record are written in the same
database transaction, and before performing a payout the consumer checks the table: if the id is

Limited-edition drop: stock reservation design (design doc)

The shop has 4 units of a limited-edition item in stock, and 5 customers (c1, c2, c3, c4, c5) try to buy
it at the same time. Each customer's checkout runs on its own server thread; the threads interleave
arbitrarily. A checkout first reserves a unit (a hold), then the customer pays to confirm the
purchase.

Holds are temporary: a hold that is not paid for expires after 4 clock ticks, and the unit goes
back into stock so that another customer can buy it. Customers can be slow to pay; the payment step
may happen at any later time.

Reserving. The checkout thread reserves with a single atomic conditional update
(UPDATE stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE count > 0); if no row is updated the customer is told the
item is sold out.

Paying. The payment service charges the customer and marks the order confirmed. It looks the order
up by customer id; whether the hold is still active or has already expired is not checked at this
point (the hold is only a soft guarantee during browsing).

Initially all customers are browsing and the stock count is 4.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types customer level tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (stock-racy)        ; checkout reads the stock level, then later writes back (value read - 1)
    (stock-atomic)      ; checkout decrements stock with one atomic conditional update
    (pay-checks-hold)   ; payment is accepted only while the customer's hold is still active
    (pay-ignores-hold)  ; payment is accepted even after the hold has expired
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-level ?lower ?higher - level)  ; stock level ?higher is one more than ?lower
    (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)
    (hold-limit ?t - tick)               ; hold age at which a hold expires
```

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t31 (31 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds

```python
    each of the times 4, 8, 12, 16, ...; a token that arrives when the bucket is full is
```

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t15 (15 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 1 clock tick of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer keeps the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips
the payout and only acknowledges the message; otherwise it credits the wallet, adds the id to the
set, and acknowledges.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:types message consumer tick)

    (dedup-none)      ; the consumer processes every delivery
    (dedup-durable)   ; processed ids are recorded in the database, atomically with the side effect
    (dedup-memory)    ; processed ids are recorded in an in-memory set of the consumer process
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (visibility-timeout ?t - tick)        ; age at which an unacknowledged message becomes visible again
    ;; --- queue ---
    (in-queue ?m - message) (visible ?m - message) (hidden ?m - message ?t - tick) (acked ?m - message)
    ;; --- consumer ---
    (idle ?w - consumer) (working ?w - consumer ?m - message) (handled ?w - consumer ?m - message)
```

**Verdict: violation.** The payout for m1 can be performed twice. The in-memory dedup set is lost when the consumer crashes after crediting the wallet but before acknowledging. The message then becomes visible again and is paid out a second time.

**Initial state:** dedup-memory, m1 in the queue and visible, m1 unprocessed and not-seen, w1 idle. t0 is the zero tick, t1 follows t0, and the visibility timeout is t1.

**Event sequence:**

1. `(receive w1 m1 t0)`: w1 is idle and m1 is visible, in the queue, and t0 is the zero tick. Now w1 is working on m1 and m1 is hidden at t0.
2. `(process-and-record-in-memory w1 m1)`: dedup-memory holds, w1 is working on m1, and m1 is unprocessed and not-seen. The wallet is credited, and m1 is now processed, seen, and handled by w1.
3. `(crash-restart-losing-memory w1 m1)`: dedup-memory holds, w1 has handled m1, and m1 is seen. w1 crashes before the ack, so the in-memory set is lost. m1 becomes not-seen again and w1 is idle.
4. `(tick m1 t0 t1)`: m1 is hidden at t0 and t1 follows t0. m1 is now hidden at t1.
5. `(reappear m1 t1)`: m1 is hidden at t1, t1 is the visibility timeout, and m1 is in the queue. m1 becomes visible again.
6. `(receive w1 m1 t0)`: w1 is idle and m1 is visible and in the queue. w1 is working on m1 again.
7. `(process-again w1 m1)`: w1 is working on m1, m1 is processed, and m1 is not-seen. The wallet is credited a second time, giving **(processed-twice m1)**.

**Root cause:** The record that m1 was processed lives only in process memory. The credit itself is durable. A crash between the credit and the ack therefore leaves a durable side effect with no durable dedup record. At-least-once redelivery then repeats the payout.

**Fix:** Record the processed message id in the payments database in the same transaction as the wallet credit (the dedup-durable mode). For example, use a unique-keyed "processed_messages" row inserted together with the credit. A redelivered message then hits the existing record and is skipped.

completion.text:
**Verdict: violation.** The cache can be left holding v2 while the database holds v3 after the writer has finished.

**Why it happens**

The design is delete-then-update with a plain set. The delete only protects against fills that happen *before* it. Two things make it fail:

- A reader can miss after the delete and read the old database value before the writer's database write lands.
- After the final database write (v2 → v3), the writer finishes without any further delete.

So a slow reader holding v2 can store it into the empty cache after the writer is done. Nothing ever removes it, because entries have no expiry.

**Event sequence** (each precondition holds at the moment of the event)

1. `(begin-delete-first v0)`: the writer starts; its next step is to delete the cache entry.
2. `(invalidate-empty v0)`: the cache is already empty; the next step is the database write.
3. `(write-db v0 v1)`: the database moves to v1; the next step is a delete.
4. `(invalidate-empty v1)`
5. `(write-db v1 v2)`: the database moves to v2.
6. `(invalidate-empty v2)`: the cache is empty and the writer is about to write v3.
7. `(read-miss v2)`: the reader misses and reads v2 from the database. It then stalls before storing.
8. `(write-db v2 v3)`: the database moves to v3; the writer reaches `writer-invalidate v3`.
9. `(finish-after-update v3)`: v3 is the final version, so the writer finishes with no delete after the last write.
10. `(fill-cache v2)`: the delayed reader stores v2, since the cache is empty and the design uses a plain set.
11. `(observe-stale v2 v3)`: the writer is done, the cache holds v2, the database holds v3, and v2 is older than v3, so `stale` holds.

**Fixes**

- Use leased sets: the delete revokes the lease, so `fill-cache-with-lease` would be blocked.
- Alternatively, add a second delete after the database write (delayed double-delete), though that only narrows the window.
- Alternatively, give cache entries a TTL to bound how long a stale value can survive.

```python
def bulk_price(unit_cents, qty):
    """Return the price in cents of `qty` items costing `unit_cents` each. The gross
```

The docstring says orders of **100 or more** items get 15% off. The code checks `qty >= 101`, so an order of exactly 100 items skips the 15% branch. It then matches `qty >= 50` and gets only 10% off.

**Counterexample:** `unit_cents=1, qty=100`

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t5 (5 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain payments)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)     ; the provider does not deduplicate requests
    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

  (:action send
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (ready ?o ?a) (first-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (ready ?o ?a)) (waiting ?o ?a) (in-flight ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t)))
  (:action lose-request
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-no-dedup
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (not (no-record ?o)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))
                 (charged ?o) (record ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response
    :parameters (?o - order)
    :precondition (response ?o)
    :effect (not (response ?o)))
  (:action receive-response
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (response ?o))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (response ?o)) (confirmed ?o)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (clock ?o ?t)) (clock ?o ?u)))
  (:action time-out-and-retry
    :parameters (?o - order ?a ?b - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t) (timeout-tick ?t) (next-attempt ?a ?b))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (clock ?o ?t)) (ready ?o ?b))))
```

system: You are a formal-methods engineer. You translate design documents into precise PDDL planning problems that a classical planner can analyse.
prompt:
--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 2 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v2. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain cache-aside)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

  (:action read-miss
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (reader-idle) (cache-empty) (db ?v))
    :effect (and (not (reader-idle)) (reader-has ?v) (lease)))
  (:action fill-cache
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (plain-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action fill-cache-with-lease
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (leased-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty) (lease))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (not (lease)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action abandon-fill
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (reader-has ?v)
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (reader-idle)))
  (:action begin-update-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action begin-delete-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-invalidate ?v)))
  (:action write-db
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-update ?v) (db ?v) (next-version ?v ?w))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (not (db ?v)) (db ?w) (writer-invalidate ?w)))
  (:action invalidate
    :parameters (?v ?x - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache ?x))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (cache ?x)) (not (lease)) (cache-empty) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action invalidate-empty
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (lease)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action finish-after-delete
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-update ?v) (final-version ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (writer-done)))
  (:action finish-after-update
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-invalidate ?v) (final-version ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (writer-done)))
  (:action observe-stale
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-done) (cache ?v) (db ?w) (older ?v ?w))
    :effect (stale)))
```

Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file

lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 3 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes. Every write carries the worker's token, and the storage
service remembers the highest token it has accepted: it rejects any write whose token is lower than
that (fencing), and accepts and records the others.

**Verdict: safe. Under this design, `(processed-twice m1)` cannot be reached.**

The design document puts the consumer in durable mode. The wallet credit and the processed-id record are committed in the same database transaction. So the initial state contains `(dedup-durable)` and not `(dedup-none)` or `(dedup-memory)`. The other initial facts are `(in-queue m1)`, `(visible m1)`, `(unprocessed m1)`, `(not-seen m1)` and `(idle w1)`.

1. **The only action that adds `(processed-twice m1)` is `process-again`.** It needs `(processed m1)` and `(not-seen m1)` to hold at the same time.

2. **Only one action can set `(processed m1)` here.** `process-without-dedup` needs `(dedup-none)` and `process-and-record-in-memory` needs `(dedup-memory)`. Both are false, and the design facts never change. That leaves `process-and-record-durably`.

3. **That action makes the two facts mutually exclusive.** In one step it adds `(processed m1)` and `(seen m1)` and deletes `(not-seen m1)`.

4. **Nothing can add `(not-seen m1)` back.** The only action that does is `crash-restart-losing-memory`, and it needs `(dedup-memory)`, which is false. The plain `crash-restart` keeps `(seen m1)`, just as a durably committed database record survives a crash.

5. **Therefore the system never reaches a state with both facts.** Before processing, `(not-seen m1)` holds but `(processed m1)` does not. After processing, `(processed m1)` holds but `(not-seen m1)` is false forever.

6. **Redelivery does not get past the check.** A message can come back after a crash, or after the 11-tick visibility timeout through `tick` and `reappear`. The later delivery always finds `(seen m1)` true and can only take `skip-duplicate` followed by `ack`.

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Limited-edition drop: stock reservation design (design doc)

The shop has 4 units of a limited-edition item in stock, and 5 customers (c1, c2, c3, c4, c5) try to buy
it at the same time. Each customer's checkout runs on its own server thread; the threads interleave
arbitrarily. A checkout first reserves a unit (a hold), then the customer pays to confirm the
purchase.

Holds are temporary: a hold that is not paid for expires after 4 clock ticks, and the unit goes
back into stock so that another customer can buy it. Customers can be slow to pay; the payment step
may happen at any later time.

Reserving. The checkout thread reserves with a single atomic conditional update
(UPDATE stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE count > 0); if no row is updated the customer is told the
item is sold out.

Paying. The payment service confirms an order only if the customer's hold is still active; payment
for an expired hold is refused and the customer must start again.

Initially all customers are browsing and the stock count is 4.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain inventory)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types customer level tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (stock-racy)        ; checkout reads the stock level, then later writes back (value read - 1)
    (stock-atomic)      ; checkout decrements stock with one atomic conditional update
    (pay-checks-hold)   ; payment is accepted only while the customer's hold is still active
    (pay-ignores-hold)  ; payment is accepted even after the hold has expired
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-level ?lower ?higher - level)  ; stock level ?higher is one more than ?lower
    (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)
    (hold-limit ?t - tick)               ; hold age at which a hold expires
    ;; --- state ---
    (stock ?q - level)                   ; current stock level
    (browsing ?c - customer)             ; customer has not started checkout
    (read-stock ?c - customer ?q - level) ; (racy) checkout of ?c read stock level ?q
    (holding ?c - customer)              ; customer holds one reserved unit
    (hold-age ?c - customer ?t - tick)
    (expired ?c - customer)              ; customer's hold expired and its unit went back to stock
    (sold ?c - customer))                ; customer's purchase is confirmed

  (:action read-stock
    :parameters (?c - customer ?q ?p - level)
    :precondition (and (stock-racy) (browsing ?c) (stock ?q) (next-level ?p ?q))
    :effect (and (not (browsing ?c)) (read-stock ?c ?q)))
  (:action write-stock
    :parameters (?c - customer ?q ?p ?cur - level ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (read-stock ?c ?q) (next-level ?p ?q) (stock ?cur) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (read-stock ?c ?q)) (not (stock ?cur)) (stock ?p) (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t)))
  (:action reserve-atomic
    :parameters (?c - customer ?q ?p - level ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (stock-atomic) (browsing ?c) (stock ?q) (next-level ?p ?q) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (browsing ?c)) (not (stock ?q)) (stock ?p) (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t)))
  (:action hold-ages
    :parameters (?c - customer ?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (hold-age ?c ?t)) (hold-age ?c ?u)))
  (:action expire-hold
    :parameters (?c - customer ?t - tick ?q ?r - level)
    :precondition (and (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t) (hold-limit ?t) (stock ?q) (next-level ?q ?r))
    :effect (and (not (holding ?c)) (not (hold-age ?c ?t)) (not (stock ?q)) (stock ?r) (expired ?c)))
  (:action pay
    :parameters (?c - customer ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t))
    :effect (and (not (holding ?c)) (not (hold-age ?c ?t)) (sold ?c)))
  (:action pay-after-expiry
    :parameters (?c - customer)
    :precondition (and (pay-ignores-hold) (expired ?c))
    :effect (and (not (expired ?c)) (sold ?c))))
```

Object names: customers c1 to c5; stock levels q0 (empty) to q4; hold ages t0 to t4.

Question: Can every one of the customers end up with a confirmed purchase, i.e. more items sold than were in stock? In the event model this means reaching a state where (and (sold c1) (sold c2) (sold c3) (sold c4) (sold c5)) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in
the design document, that ends in such a state: a list of ground actions such as "(action arg1 arg2)".
Every action's precondition must hold at the moment it occurs. If it cannot happen under this design,
say so.

End your answer with a JSON object in a ```json block, either
{"verdict": "violation", "trace": ["(action arg ...)", ...]}
or
{"verdict": "safe"}

completion.text:
**Verdict: safe.** Under this design, at most 4 customers can end up with a confirmed purchase. A state where all 5 are sold cannot be reached.

**Which events are possible.** The design uses one atomic conditional update and checks the hold at payment. So the model has `(stock-atomic)` and `(pay-checks-hold)`, and does not have `(stock-racy)` or `(pay-ignores-hold)`. That rules out three events:
- `read-stock` needs `stock-racy`.
- `write-stock` needs a `read-stock` fact, which only `read-stock` creates.
- `pay-after-expiry` needs `pay-ignores-hold`.

The only events left are `reserve-atomic`, `hold-ages`, `expire-hold` and `pay`.

**Invariant.** Let S be the current stock level, H the number of customers holding a unit, and P the number of customers sold. Then S + H + P = 4 at all times.
- At the start, S = 4, H = 0 and P = 0.
- `reserve-atomic` lowers S by 1 and raises H by 1. It needs a level one below S, so it cannot run when S = 0.
- `hold-ages` changes only the hold's age.
- `expire-hold` lowers H by 1 and raises S by 1. The customer becomes `expired`.
- `pay` lowers H by 1 and raises P by 1. The unit leaves stock for good.

Each event keeps the sum at 4, so P ≤ 4.

**No second chance after expiry.** A customer whose hold expires is no longer `browsing` or `holding`. So they can never reserve again or pay. The returned unit can only go to a customer who is still browsing.

**Conclusion.** At most 4 of the 5 customers can reach `sold`. The goal of all five sold is unreachable, so this design has no overselling violation.


prompt:
--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 11 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

the token is logged for auditing only.

--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 1 clock tick of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer keeps the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips
the payout and only acknowledges the message; otherwise it credits the wallet, adds the id to the
set, and acknowledges.

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t3 (3 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

```pddl
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---

    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---

    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt

    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
```

```pddl
    :parameters (?t ?u - tick)
```

Question: Can a write from a worker whose lease had expired be applied after the other worker's write (corrupting the file)? In the event model this means reaching a state where (corrupted) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in
the design document, that ends in such a state: a list of ground actions such as "(action arg1 arg2)".
Every action's precondition must hold at the moment it occurs. If it cannot happen under this design,
say so.

End your answer with a JSON object in a ```json block, either
{"verdict": "violation", "trace": ["(action arg ...)", ...]}
or
{"verdict": "safe"}

completion.text:
**Verdict: safe.** Under this design, no sequence of events can reach `(corrupted)`. The lease check can be defeated by a stall, but fencing always stops the stale write.

**Design facts in force.** The initial state has `(fencing)` and `(checks-lease)`. It does not have `(no-fencing)` or `(no-lease-check)`. So the only write actions that can ever run are `write-fenced`, `write-fenced-over-newer` and `reject-stale-write`. The two unfenced write actions can never run.

**Invariant.** Storage's `max-seen` token is always at least as high as every token in a `wrote` fact.
- At the start it holds: `max-seen k0` is true and nothing has been written.
- Only `write-fenced` adds a `wrote` fact. It needs `max-seen j` with `j ≤ k`. It then sets `max-seen` to `k` and adds `wrote k`. So `max-seen` never decreases, and it always covers the newest token written.
- No other action changes `max-seen` or adds a `wrote` fact.

**Why corruption cannot happen.** `write-fenced-over-newer` is the only remaining action that sets `(corrupted)`. It needs `max-seen j`, `j ≤ k`, and `wrote m` with `k < m`. By the invariant, `m ≤ j`, so it would need `m ≤ j ≤ k < m`, which is impossible. So `(corrupted)` can never be reached.

**The dangerous interleaving, checked.** This is the race the lease check alone cannot prevent:
1. c1 acquires the lock with token k1.
2. c1 checks its lease, which is still valid, and becomes ready to write.
3. c1 stalls. Its lease ages to t11 and expires.
4. c2 acquires the lock with token k2 and writes. Storage now has `max-seen k2`.
5. c1 wakes and tries to write with k1.

At step 5, `write-fenced` and `write-fenced-over-newer` both need `max-seen ≤ k1`, so neither applies. Only `reject-stale-write` (k1 < k2) applies, and storage rejects c1's write.

So the lease check by itself is not enough, because a stall after the check defeats it. Fencing is what makes the design safe.

```json
{"verdict": "safe"}
```

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t3 (3 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging. The provider treats every request it receives as a new payment: it approves the request
and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for
bookkeeping only; the provider does not use it to detect repeats.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-1)
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    ;; --- static counters ---

    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t

    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---

    ;; --- provider ---

    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored

    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t - tick)

  (:action accept-2

  (:action accept-1
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-3) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (not (no-record ?o)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-3
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)

  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)

  (:action lose-response
    :parameters (?o - order)
    :precondition (response ?o)
    :effect (not (response ?o)))
  (:action receive-response
```

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in

completion.text:
**Yes, the card can be charged twice.** The provider treats every request as a new payment and ignores the order number. So a delayed original request and its retry are both charged.

**Model setup.** Because the provider does no duplicate detection, only `mode-1` holds. That leaves `accept-2` as the only enabled accept action, and it never checks for an existing record.

- **Initial state:** `(ready o1 a0)`, `(no-record o1)`, `(uncharged o1)`.
- **Static facts:**
  - `first-tick t0`
  - `next-tick` t0→t1→t2→t3
  - `timeout-tick t3`
  - `next-attempt` a0→a1→a2

**Event sequence:**

1. `(send o1 a0 t0)`: the client sends attempt a0. Now `(waiting o1 a0)`, `(in-flight o1 a0)` and `(clock o1 t0)` hold.
2. `(tick o1 a0 t0 t1)`: the timer advances. The a0 request is delayed in the network.
3. `(tick o1 a0 t1 t2)`
4. `(tick o1 a0 t2 t3)`
5. `(time-out-and-retry o1 a0 a1 t3)`: the client gives up on a0 and becomes `(ready o1 a1)`. The a0 request is still in flight.
6. `(send o1 a1 t0)`: the retry a1 is now also in flight.
7. `(accept-2 o1 a0)`: the delayed a0 request reaches the provider and is approved.
8. `(charge o1 a0)`: the card is charged once, giving `(charged o1)`.
9. `(accept-2 o1 a1)`: the retry reaches the provider. Nothing checks for a repeat, so it is approved too.
10. `(charge-again o1 a1)`: the card is charged a second time, giving `(charged-twice o1)`.

**Root cause:** the provider has no idempotency check keyed on the order. Combined with client retries and arbitrary network delay, one order can be charged more than once. The fix is to have the provider deduplicate requests by order number or idempotency key, as `accept-1` and `replay-2` do in `mode-3`. A check alone (`mode-2`) is not enough: `accept-3` leaves `no-record` set, so two copies could both be approved before either is charged. The provider must reserve the key at the moment it accepts a request, before charging.


--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
calling the bank API (an external side effect that cannot be undone), then acknowledges the message
so the queue deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 1 clock tick of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer keeps the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips
the payout and only acknowledges the message; otherwise it performs the payout, adds the id to the
set, and acknowledges.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types message consumer tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    (mode-1)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (visibility-timeout ?t - tick)        ; age at which an unacknowledged message becomes visible again
    ;; --- queue ---
    (in-queue ?m - message) (visible ?m - message) (hidden ?m - message ?t - tick) (acked ?m - message)
    ;; --- consumer ---
    (idle ?w - consumer) (working ?w - consumer ?m - message) (handled ?w - consumer ?m - message)
    ;; --- effects of processing ---
    (unprocessed ?m - message) (processed ?m - message) (processed-twice ?m - message)
    (not-seen ?m - message) (seen ?m - message))

  (:action receive
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?w) (visible ?m) (in-queue ?m) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?w)) (not (visible ?m)) (working ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t)))
  (:action process-2
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (mode-3) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-3
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (mode-2) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)
                 (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-1
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (mode-1) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)
                 (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action skip-duplicate
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-again
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (processed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (processed-twice ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
```

```python
def run_length(xs):
    """Run-length encode `xs`: split it into maximal runs of equal consecutive values and
    return a flat list [v1, c1, v2, c2, ...] where run number k consists of ck copies
    of the value vk, in order.
    """
    out = []
    i = 0
    while i <= len(xs):
        j = i
        while j < len(xs) and xs[j] == xs[i]:

        out.append(xs[i])
        out.append(j - i)
```

completion.text:
Yes, there is a failing input. The bug is the loop condition `while i <= len(xs)`, which should be `i < len(xs)`.

**Empty input `xs = []`:**
- `i = 0` and `len(xs) = 0`, so `0 <= 0` is true and the loop body runs.
- The inner `while` exits at once, because `j < len(xs)` is false and short-circuits.
- `out.append(xs[i])` then evaluates `xs[0]` on an empty list and raises `IndexError`.
- The docstring requires `[]`, since an empty list has no runs.

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t15 (15 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates

    (dedup-none)     ; the provider does not deduplicate requests
    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---

    :precondition (and (ready ?o ?a) (first-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (ready ?o ?a)) (waiting ?o ?a) (in-flight ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t)))
  (:action lose-request

    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))

    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))

    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))

    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))
```

**Verdict: violation.** The card can be charged twice for order o1.

**Which deduplication mode applies.** The design doc says the provider looks the key up and writes the record only "once the charge has succeeded." That matches `(dedup-racy)`. In that mode, `accept-new-racy` checks `(no-record o1)` but does not clear it. Only `charge` removes it. So two in-flight attempts can both be approved before either charge writes the record.

**How it fails.**
1. Attempt a0 is sent but is delayed in the network.
2. The client's timer reaches t15 and it retries with a1. The a0 request is still in flight.
3. The provider accepts a0. No record exists, and accepting does not reserve the key.
4. The provider then accepts a1. There is still no record, so it is approved too.
5. The provider charges a0. Only now is the record written.
6. a1 is already approved, so `charge-again` fires and the card is charged a second time.

**Initial state:** `(ready o1 a0)`, `(no-record o1)`, `(uncharged o1)`, `(dedup-racy)`, `(first-tick t0)`, `(timeout-tick t15)`, the next-tick chain t0 to t15, and next-attempt a0→a1→a2.

**Fix.** Reserve the key atomically at lookup time, which is `dedup-atomic`. Then the second request would find a reservation and could not be approved.

--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 6 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v6. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database

    (writer-done)

  (:action abandon-fill
    :parameters (?v - version)

    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (reader-idle)))
  (:action begin-update-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action begin-delete-first

    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-invalidate ?v)))
  (:action write-db
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-update ?v) (db ?v) (next-version ?v ?w))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (not (db ?v)) (db ?w) (writer-invalidate ?w)))
  (:action invalidate

    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (cache ?x)) (not (lease)) (cache-empty) (writer-update ?v)))
```

**Verdict: violation.** The cache can be left holding v7 after the database has reached v8 and the writer has finished.

The design deletes the cache entry before writing the database, and the reader always stores what it read. A reader that misses in the gap between the delete and the database write reads the old version. It can then store that old version after the writer's last write. No later delete removes it, and entries never expire, so the stale value stays permanently.

**Event sequence:**

1. The writer runs updates 1–7 normally. For each update it deletes the entry from the cache, which is already empty, and then writes the next version. This takes the database from v0 to v7.
2. For update 8, the writer deletes the entry from the cache, which is still empty (`invalidate-empty v7`).
3. The reader misses and reads v7 from the database (`read-miss v7`).
4. The writer writes v8 to the database (`write-db v7 v8`) and finishes (`finish-after-update v8`).
5. The delayed reader stores v7 in the cache (`fill-cache v7`). This is allowed because the cache is empty and the design uses plain set.
6. The writer is done, the cache holds v7 and the database holds v8, so the state is stale (`observe-stale v7 v8`).

**Fix:** Delete the cache entry after the database write as well (update-then-delete, or delete twice). In addition, use leased or versioned sets, so that a fill whose lease was revoked by a delete is rejected.

Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 5 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer keeps the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips
the payout and only acknowledges the message; otherwise it credits the wallet, adds the id to the
set, and acknowledges.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state

```pddl
  (:domain queue)
  (:objects
    m1 - message
    w1 - consumer
    t0 t1 t2 t3 t4 t5 - tick)
  (:init
    ;; design fact: the dedup set lives in process memory and is lost on crash
    (mode-1)
    ;; static counters
    (zero-tick t0)
    (next-tick t0 t1) (next-tick t1 t2) (next-tick t2 t3) (next-tick t3 t4) (next-tick t4 t5)
    (visibility-timeout t5)
    ;; queue
    (in-queue m1) (visible m1)
    ;; consumer
    (idle w1)
    ;; processing state
    (unprocessed m1) (not-seen m1))
  (:goal (processed-twice m1)))
```

I chose `(mode-1)` as the design fact because of how the design keeps its deduplication set:

- **The set is in process memory.** The consumer stores the ids of paid-out messages in its own memory. When the process crashes and restarts, that memory is lost.
- **`crash-1` models that loss.** It is the only action that resets `seen` to `not-seen`, and it requires `mode-1`.
- **`mode-2` would be wrong.** It keeps deduplication, but the dedup record survives a crash, as a durable store would.
- **`mode-3` would be wrong.** It has no deduplication check at all.

The visibility timeout of 5 ticks is encoded as `(visibility-timeout t5)`. Message ages run from `t0` to `t5`, with `t0` as the starting age.

--- Design document ---
Limited-edition drop: stock reservation design (design doc)

The shop has 2 units of a limited-edition item in stock, and 3 customers (c1, c2, c3) try to buy
it at the same time. Each customer's checkout runs on its own server thread; the threads interleave
arbitrarily. A checkout first reserves a unit (a hold), then the customer pays to confirm the
purchase.

Holds are temporary: a hold that is not paid for expires after 2 clock ticks, and the unit goes
back into stock so that another customer can buy it. Customers can be slow to pay; the payment step
may happen at any later time.

Reserving. The checkout thread reads the current stock count from the database, checks that it is
above zero, and then, as a separate statement, writes back the count it read minus one. No lock or
transaction spans the read and the write.

Paying. The payment service confirms an order only if the customer's hold is still active; payment
for an expired hold is refused and the customer must start again.

Initially all customers are browsing and the stock count is 2.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:types customer level tick)
  (:predicates

    (mode-4)

    :effect (and (not (browsing ?c)) (read-1 ?c ?q)))
```

Question: Can every one of the customers end up with a confirmed purchase, i.e. more items sold than were in stock? In the event model this means reaching a state where (and (sold c1) (sold c2) (sold c3)) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in

Every action's precondition must hold at the moment it occurs. If it cannot happen under this design,

completion.text:
**Verdict: violation.** All three customers can end up with a confirmed purchase even though only 2 units exist.

**Which design facts hold.** Reserving is a plain read followed by a separate write, so `mode-1` holds. The atomic `reserve-1` path (`mode-4`) does not. Payment for an expired hold is refused, so `mode-2` (`pay-1`) is false. `mode-3` is not used by any action.

**How it happens: a lost update.** No lock spans the read and the write. So all three checkout threads can read the stock count while it is still 2. Each then writes back 2 − 1 = 1, overwriting the others' decrements. Every write gives that customer an active hold, and each customer pays before the hold ages out.

**Event sequence:**

1. `(read-1 c1 q2 q1)`: c1 reads stock = 2, which is above zero.
2. `(read-1 c2 q2 q1)`: c2 reads stock = 2.
3. `(read-1 c3 q2 q1)`: c3 reads stock = 2.
4. `(write-stock c1 q2 q1 q2 t0)`: c1 writes 1 and gets a hold. Stock is now 1.
5. `(write-stock c2 q2 q1 q1 t0)`: c2 writes 1, which is a lost update. c2 holds a unit and stock stays 1.
6. `(write-stock c3 q2 q1 q1 t0)`: c3 writes 1, another lost update. c3 holds a unit and stock stays 1.
7. `(pay c1 t0)`: c1's hold is active and age 0, so the purchase is confirmed.
8. `(pay c2 t0)`: confirmed.
9. `(pay c3 t0)`: confirmed.

The result is 3 units sold from a stock of 2, and the database still shows 1 unit available.

**Note on steps 5 and 6.** In these steps the current level and the written level are the same (q1). Standard STRIPS semantics apply deletes before adds, so `(stock q1)` still holds after each write.

**Fix.** Make the reservation atomic. Either use a conditional decrement such as `UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0` and check the affected row count, or wrap the read and write in a transaction with a row lock. That is the `reserve-1` path in the model.

```json

```

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 5 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain lease-lock)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (fencing)          ; storage rejects writes whose token is older than the newest it has seen
    (no-fencing)       ; storage accepts every write
    (checks-lease)     ; a client checks it still holds the lease right before writing
    (no-lease-check)   ; a client writes whenever it believes it holds the lock
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---
    (max-seen ?k - token)                ; newest token storage has seen (used with fencing)
    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
    (corrupted))                         ; an older holder's write was applied after a newer holder's write

  (:action acquire
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?l - token ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?c) (lock-free) (last-issued ?k) (next-token ?k ?l) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?c)) (not (lock-free)) (not (last-issued ?k)) (last-issued ?l)
                 (holder ?c) (believes ?c) (token-of ?c ?l) (lease-age ?t)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (lease-age ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (lease-age ?t)) (lease-age ?u)))
  (:action expire
    :parameters (?c - client ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (holder ?c) (lease-age ?t) (lease-limit ?t))
    :effect (and (not (holder ?c)) (not (lease-age ?t)) (lock-free) (lease-expired ?c)))
  (:action prepare-write
    :parameters (?c - client)
    :precondition (and (no-lease-check) (believes ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action check-lease-and-prepare-write
    :parameters (?c - client)
    :precondition (and (checks-lease) (believes ?c) (holder ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action write-unfenced
    :parameters (?c - client ?k - token)
    :precondition (and (no-fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (wrote ?k)))
  (:action write-unfenced-over-newer
```

**Verdict: violation.** The payout for m1 can be performed twice.

**Which mode applies.** The design says the consumer "performs the payout for every message it receives, then acknowledges it." Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an

or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t11 (11 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

**Yes, the card can be charged twice.** The design says the provider "looks the key up" and only "once the charge has succeeded, writes the record." That is the `dedup-racy` mode. The lookup and the record write are separate steps, so a retry that arrives during the first attempt's charge also finds no record. It gets approved and charges the card again.

**Event sequence:**

1. `(send o1 a0 t0)`: the client sends attempt a0 and starts its timer at t0.
2. `(accept-new-racy o1 a0)`: the provider finds no record and approves a0. No reservation is written, so `no-record o1` still holds.
3. `(tick o1 a0 t0 t1)` through `(tick o1 a0 t10 t11)`: the provider's charge for a0 is slow, so no response arrives and the client's timer reaches t11.
4. `(time-out-and-retry o1 a0 a1 t11)`: the client gives up on a0 and gets ready to send a1.
5. `(send o1 a1 t0)`: the client sends retry a1 with the same idempotency key.
6. `(accept-new-racy o1 a1)`: on another worker thread, the lookup again finds no record, because a0 has not finished charging. a1 is approved.
7. `(charge o1 a0)`: a0's charge succeeds and the record is written.
8. `(charge-again o1 a1)`: a1 was already approved, so it charges the card a second time, giving `charged-twice o1`.

**Root cause:** the idempotency check is a check-then-act race. The fix is to reserve the key atomically in the same step as the lookup (the `dedup-atomic` mode), for example with an insert-if-absent "in progress" record. A request that finds a reservation should then wait for the stored result or replay it, not charge.

waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 5 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Once a worker holds the lock it writes the file. The storage service accepts any write;
the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    (mode-1)
    (mode-4)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---

    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
    (corrupted))                         ; an older holder's write was applied after a newer holder's write

    :effect (and (not (idle ?c)) (not (lock-free)) (not (last-issued ?k)) (last-issued ?l)

  (:action write-4
```

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
calling the bank API (an external side effect that cannot be undone), then acknowledges the message
so the queue deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 3 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer records the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
table in the payments database. The payout ledger entry and the id record are written in the same
database transaction, and before performing a payout the consumer checks the table: if the id is
there it skips the payout and only acknowledges the message.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

